title: How NPR makes race calls in the 2026 election
description: Voters enter a polling station at Midtow
body:
Voters enter a polling station at Midtown Mall on October 31, 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America
    

   
   How NPR makes race calls in the 2026 election   Voters are voting, ballots are being counted and results are starting to come in for 435 House races, 35 Senate races and 36 gubernatorial contests as well as ballot measures and thousands of state legislative seats. But how will NPR call races on election night? Determining a winner in any of the many races across the country is a big job. That's why NPR partners with the Associated Press — and has for many years — to ensure that races are called accurately.   The Associated Press has been calling races since 1848 and even now, nearly 180 years later, the process for making those calls is pretty simple. Here's how the AP explains its race calling process:   
   Race callers collaborate with analysts who focus on statewide races, such as those for U.S. Senate and governor, and elections for the U.S. House of Representatives. The decision editors on AP's Decision Team sign off on every race call for president, U.S. Senate and governor, as well as races of significance for U.S. House.    Together, they are looking at far more than just the overall vote totals. They study the incoming vote county by county. In states where the information is available, they look at the vote by type of ballot: cast in person at polling places, or in advance by mail or in person. They are also in constant contact with AP's vote count team, in search of the latest information about what's been counted so far and how many ballots may still be left to count.   Once AP has an idea of how many ballots are outstanding versus how many have been counted, their staff can start to tabulate the likelihood of a certain winner being victorious in a certain contest based on a lot of different factors: where the ballots that are outstanding are coming from, what the makeup of those communities looks like and even, how the individual chose to vote.   
   For NPR's part, once the AP calls a race, we will alert our broadcast and digital audiences on air as part of special coverage and online through digital stories. We also ensure that our hundreds of member stations also have access to that information. We will use AP's data to populate our election results pages so viewers can keep track, in real time.   How are races called when not all votes have been counted?   But sometimes, races might be called without all — or even most — of the vote counted. How is that possible?   The Associated Press explained in 2024 that it uses that same calculation of ballots, external factors and other data to inform its decisions.   In almost all cases, races can be called well before 100% of the votes have been counted. The AP's team of election journalists and analysts will call a race as soon as a clear winner can be determined. That may sound obvious, but it is the guiding principle that drives the organization's election race-calling process.   The AP's race calls are not predictions and are not based on speculation. They are declarations based on an analysis of vote results and other election data that one candidate has emerged as the winner and that no other candidate in the race will be able to overtake the winner once all the votes have been counted.   It sounds simple, right? The AP won't call races until "a clear winner can be determined." But that doesn't always require all of the votes for every precinct for every race. Sometimes it's all about the math: can this candidate feasibly win with the votes outstanding in the places they are yet to be counted? And that raises another, really important point.    The AP – and therefore NPR – will not project races. The team at the AP will wait until it has certainty to call raises and that is why its race calls are trusted by hundreds of news organizations, including NPR. Because they wait until there is surety, even if it means waiting just a bit longer to be sure.   
   On an ethical note, NPR will not make race calls just because a candidate declares victory, nor will NPR use a concession speech or statement to make a race call either. That is true of the Associated Press as well:   AP does not make projections or name apparent or likely winners. If our race callers cannot definitively say a candidate has won, we do not engage in speculation. For example, AP did not call the closely contested race in 2000 between George W. Bush and Al Gore – we stood behind our assessment that the margin in Florida made it too close to say who won.    AP only calls a race when we are fully confident that race has been won – defined most simply as the moment the trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory.    When AP makes a race call, we back it up with transparent reporting into the research and analysis that led us to say with certainty who has won. This explanatory journalism is as much a hallmark of our coverage of U.S. elections as the race calls themselves.   While election night is the start of these race calls, it likely will not be the end. Counting voters can take a while. Race calls will be tabulated to determine the balance of power in the Senate and the House of Representatives. NPR will cover all major race calls and provide ongoing coverage on air and online of just how the 2026 election shakes out.

title: Coal no longer king in Navajo Nation presidential election
description: For the first time in decades, there's no pro-coal candidate for Navajo Nation president. Coal has been an important part of the economy, but v
body:
For the first time in decades, there's no pro-coal candidate for Navajo Nation president. Coal has been an important part of the economy, but voter sentiment is changing.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  Among the election races that we're watching is the one for president of the Navajo Nation. The tribe counts nearly half a million enrolled members, and this year's election is unusual. It's the first in recent memory without a candidate who supports the coal industry. Coal has been the tribe's economic bedrock for generations. KJZZ's Gabriel Pietrorazio reports.GABRIEL PIETRORAZIO, BYLINE: Sitting President Buu Nygren was a delegate to the 2024 Democratic National Convention. But when it comes to coal, he aligns with President Trump, who's reversing his predecessor's efforts to phase out use of the fossil fuel. During an annual address in January, Nygren promised to keep the last remaining coal mine on the reservation open and support the sole power plant it fuels.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)BUU NYGREN: Because those are hundreds and hundreds of jobs. Those are millions and millions of dollars of revenue that the Navajo Nation receives.PIETRORAZIO: And he pointed out that a lot of people on the reservation still rely on coal to heat homes located far from conventional energy grids.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)NYGREN: That's coal that some of you haul and get for free from some of our chapters and...PIETRORAZIO: But voters rejected Nygren. He and 13 other candidates didn't get past the primary. Justin Jones did.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JUSTIN JONES: I'm opposed to coal mining.PIETRORAZIO: Jones is an attorney and an ex-liaison for a coal mine in New Mexico.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JONES: I'm opposed to any form of mining that's where a shovel will go, blast it and get resources out.PIETRORAZIO: Jones' opponent is Crystalyne Curley, who is currently speaker of the Navajo Nation Council.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)CRYSTALYNE CURLEY: Coal is dying. It's not coming back. So you do need an administration that will say, this is the new plan to move forward.PIETRORAZIO: President Nygren did the opposite, taking a selfie with President Trump last year at the White House when Trump signed an executive order aimed at saving the, quote, "beautiful, clean coal industry." That really hurt Nygren's reelection chances, says Andrew Curley, an assistant professor at the University of Arizona, who wrote a book on Navajo energy industry politics. He's not related to Crystalyne Curley but has campaigned on her behalf.ANDREW CURLEY: Based on my conversations with voters, people were upset. It kind of reflected a politics I think a lot of people on the reservation reject and is unattuned to the real struggles, real challenges for the coal economy.PIETRORAZIO: Curley himself was a candidate for Navajo president this cycle but didn't advance beyond the primary. In his eyes, it's significant that candidates no longer feel like they need to embrace the coal industry.A CURLEY: And I think that's good. I think it's good that both sides are kind of moving in this direction to think about the land in terms of sustainability, not just resources and extraction.PIETRORAZIO: Forty-four-year-old Dailin Long lives on the reservation, near the last remaining coal mine. The Trump administration recently approved it for expansion. In the past, he's voted for President Nygren, but now he's glad Nygren is no longer on the ballot.DAILIN LONG: Our hope was that he would establish a legacy that speaks to our generation, and it seems that, unfortunately, he kind of just blended in with the status quo.PIETRORAZIO: Long's family could be displaced by the coal mine. After listening to what the remaining candidates have to say about coal, he just hopes it's not campaign rhetoric yet again.LONG: I really do hope they take it to heart and really consider we need an energy policy that works for us.PIETRORAZIO: For now, the Navajo Nation owns and continues to operate a major coal mining company, with mines in New Mexico, Wyoming and Montana.For NPR News I'm Gabriel Pietrorazio.

title: It's Election Day. Control of Congress is on the line, and what else you need to know
description: In an aerial view, voters wait in line o
body:
In an aerial view, voters wait in line on the last day of early in-person voting at the Franklin County Board of Elections on Nov. 1 in Columbus, Ohio.
                
                    Jon Cherry/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jon Cherry/Getty Images
    

   
      It's finally here. Election Day. Today, voting officially ends.   No more talk of polls. Now, it's about results.   More than 59 million people have already cast ballots. That's nearly half of the total ballots cast in the last midterm election. Democrats hold a double-digit advantage going into today, based on available data from early voting.   
   But a major key today will be how many Republicans show up to the polls. There are so many red states and districts in play, and the GOP votes overwhelmingly in person on Election Day.   Democrats are favored to win the House. They only have to flip three seats for control, and the landscape has shifted considerably, even in the past month, in favor of Democrats.   Republicans tried to insulate themselves with rare, mid-decade redistricting. But it likely won't be enough to help the party keep the chamber.   In the Senate, the outcome is anyone's guess. Democrats need to flip four seats to gain control of the Senate, something that was unthinkable at the beginning of this cycle. But strong Democratic recruits and a difficult national political environment for Republicans have made it a possibility.   Democrats are favored to flip one seat — North Carolina. But beyond that, the races are either toss-ups or Republicans are slight favorites. And the elections are taking place on GOP turf. Apart from Maine, the five toss-ups held by Republicans are in states Trump won by double digits in 2024.   
   That's why Trump has been in so many red states ahead of Election Day to try and turn out his base. Republicans' top target is Michigan. If they win that, Democrats' calculus changes.   High Republican turnout could limit Democrats to one pick up. Low turnout among Republican voters could see a wipeout of up to six or seven seats — and result in Democratic control of the Senate.   There are a lot of variables for how things will go today. Results will start to come in at 6 p.m. ET in Kentucky and Indiana, and then it will be off to the races. And while everyone wants to know the results on election night, in many places the results will not be known. So patience is key as states count votes in what are expected to be many close races.   
   It could take days. It could take weeks, but ballots are being counted and results are coming soon.    Loading...

title: 'Messy,' 'divided' and 'scary': swing voters rate the country ahead of Election Day
description: Voters Lee, Wally, Theresa, and Gerald.
body:
Voters Lee, Wally, Theresa, and Gerald.
                
                    Tara Anand for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tara Anand for NPR
    

   
   Gerald and Wally both voted for President Trump in 2024, helping him with the state of Georgia. Their votes in 2026 illustrate the challenges the president and his party face in today's midterms.   Gerald is still all in, giving Trump an A+++. He cast his ballot on the first day of early voting in Georgia for Republicans Mike Collins for Senate and Rick Jackson for governor.   "Red all the way down the ballot," Gerald said. "There was one instance where there was nothing but a Democrat running unopposed and I preferred to write my own name in, because I refuse to give a Democrat my vote."    
   Wally, on the other hand, represents a fraying of the Trump coalition. Every time he's been asked since March, he's given the president an F.   "I just don't think that he's an effective leader and I thought that as Americans we'd do so much better," he said.   Wally said inflation is the top issue influencing his vote, but he doesn't have a lot of hope that any one politician or any one election can fix it. He also voted early in Georgia for the Democratic Senate incumbent Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms — a vote against Trump and MAGA as much as anything else.   He gives Democrats and Republicans in Congress an F as well.   "I think these people are essentially stealing money from the American public and we need wholesale change in this midterm, and we also need a big change for the next presidential election," he said.   Wally and Gerald are among a group of swing voters in swing states NPR has been checking in with regularly as part of a long-term reporting project called Swing Shift. NPR has agreed not to use their full names so they can speak freely about politics, without fear of personal or professional repercussions.   
   All of the Swing Shift voters have cast a ballot for President Trump over the past decade. Most of them voted for him just two years ago.   When Americans cast their votes in the midterm elections, they'll have the chance to weigh in on the state of the country, nearly two years into President Trump's second term in office.   Asked for one word or phrase to describe how they are feeling, Swing Shift voters used words like "messy," "divided," "disarray," and "scary. "    Loading... 
   In the week before Election Day, their assessment of Trump's performance on the job roughly aligns with national polls: most were unhappy or underwhelmed, often citing the war in Iran and high energy prices as major concerns. Only two of the 11 Swing Shift voters told NPR they were happy with Trump's second term.   Theresa, a Pennsylvania voter who voted for former President Joe Biden in 2020, then President Trump in 2024, said she would give the president a C-.   "Because he said the war was only going to be a few weeks. And we knew that was not the case," she said.    
   Lee from Nevada, one of the voters happy with Trump, still voiced concerns about the war with Iran. He gave Trump's performance in office this term an A-.   "Because the war in Iran is taking kind of long," he said.   When NPR first spoke to Lee, he was out of work. Now, with a new job, his outlook on the economy has improved. He said he's gotten even more Republican since the last election and more suspicious of Democrats.   Meanwhile, Quintero, a Biden to Trump voter, also from Nevada, told NPR he is swinging back to Democrats in this year's midterms.   That's the challenge for Republicans: two years in, the Trump 2024 base isn't supplying reliable Republican votes.    Loading... 
   Trump hangs over every race — but he isn't on the ballot   Even as this election, like all midterms, has turned into a referendum on the president and his policies, he isn't on the ballot. So the question is how their feelings about Trump and his presidency will translate to votes for the House, Senate and governors.   In Pennsylvania, the Swing Shift voters are divided: three out of four voted for Trump in 2024. Now, three of them plan to vote for Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is seeking re-election.    
   "I might get in there and change my mind again. But at this point, it is going to be with the politician that we're familiar with, which is Shapiro," Theresa said.   In the northern suburbs of Philadelphia, Stephen lives in one of the most competitive House districts in the country, Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District. Incumbent Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick has survived a Democratic wave before, and Stephen is willing to stick with him.   "I would still re-elect Brian Fitzpatrick but everything else, I would say maybe Democratic or…maybe do a write in," Stephen said.   
   At the top of the ticket, though, he's voting for Shapiro.   Only John from Philadelphia said he voted for the Republican in the governor's race. He said he feels like the country is "teetering" and he isn't happy with either party. He follows the news closely and sees where the political tides are headed.   "I think there will be a lot of investigations, a lot of impeachment talk and a lot of gridlock in Washington," John said of a possible Democratic win in the midterms. "And I don't know if we can afford that right now. So my word to describe the state of the country is 'anxious.'"

title: Four types of House races to watch on election night to know how it might go
description: People cast their ballots on the first d
body:
People cast their ballots on the first day of early voting for the midterm elections, in New York, on Oct. 24, 2026.
                
                    Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Democrats appear poised to retake control of the House on Tuesday. If they do, will their majority be built upon a blue wave or a tiny trickle? A previous NPR analysis found both parties spending deep and wide in a competitive landscape that spans 70 districts, ranging from longtime tossups to newly-competitive seats in deeply conservative areas.   Republicans came into Election Day with a narrow 218-214 seat advantage in the House and facing severe headwinds as the party in power. This midterm cycle has also seen a record number of departures from Congress, and polls show voters aren't happy about things like the economy and the ongoing war in Iran.   
   So what separates a good night for Democrats from a blue wave that sees dozens of House seats change hands? Here's NPR's cheat sheet to four types of House races to watch as results come in:   Early polls closing   The first results of the night with national implications will likely be from Kentucky's 6th Congressional District (KY-06) and Indiana's 5th (IN-05), two districts where polls close first (in the 6 p.m. ET hour) and whose 2024 margins for President Trump (15 and 17 points, respectively) could act as a preview for how much voters have soured on Republicans.   Democrats and Republicans alike have spent heavily in the Kentucky race, where Democrat Zach Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado, so the increased investment is worth noting as a factor on the outcome. If Democrats flip one or both of these races, then it will likely be a long night for the GOP.   
   Florida also counts and reports its votes quickly, and is home to more than a half dozen races that are viewed as toss-ups or slightly favor one party or the other, so as these districts have projected winners there will be more insight into other races across the country.   Like the Kentucky contest, both parties have spent significant sums in races like the open seat in FL-22 with Democrat Pia Dandiya facing off against Republican Casey Askar and incumbent Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz versus Republican Scott Singer in the newly-redrawn FL-25 race.   
   Other races to watch: FL-27, NC-11, SC-01, VA-01   Last-minute big spending   In the final seven days of the midterms, a handful of House races have seen more than $10 million in ad spending, according to data from AdImpact. It's a sign of where both parties think the saying "It all comes down to turnout!" is more than a cliche. That includes districts in Michigan, such as MI-07, where progressive Democrat William Lawrence is challenging incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in a seat that Trump carried by just over one percent in 2024 and the open MI-10, where Democrat Christina Hines faces Republican Mike Bouchard.   New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in NY-17 could be one of the rare Republicans who holds on to his seat thanks in part to his party's ad spending advantage in the closing stretch against Democrat Cait Conley.   
   Three of Iowa's four House races, IA-01, IA-02 and IA-03 are on the list of most expensive, in part because of the competitive governor and U.S. Senate races that are also on the ballot and driving up turnout.   Other races to watch: CO-08, PA-01, WA-03, WI-03   Redistricting   This year's Supreme Court decision rolling back part of the Voting Rights Act led to many Republican-led states redrawing their House maps to eliminate districts that favor Democrats in a typical election year – but this year is not typical.   Now, the political environment has deteriorated so much that seats like AL-02, held by Democrat Shomari Figures, OH-09 held by Democrat Marcy Kaptur and NC-01 held by Democrat Don Davis are all considered toss-ups at best and favoring the Democrats at worst for Republicans.   In Texas, Latino voters seem poised to swing back to Democratic candidates and could prevent Republican Eric Flores from flipping the seat held by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in TX-34 or Tano Tijerina from unseating Democratic incumbent Henry Cuellar in TX-28.   
   Other races to watch: CA-22, FL-09, FL-14, TX-35   The outer edges of the map   As results continue to be reported, one thing to watch is how far into conservative communities the increased support for Democrats can go.   
   One race that has received a surprising amount of ad attention is in Arkansas's 2nd district (AR-02), where incumbent Republican Rep. French Hill faces a well-known challenger in Democrat Chris Jones. By the time polls close, closer to $10 million will have been spent in the final months on the Little Rock-based seat that Trump carried by 15 points in 2024.   There are also many districts in states that redrew their maps where the Republican gerrymander could backfire, like Ohio. In both OH-10 held by Republican Mike Turner and OH-15 held by Republican Mike Carey, Trump won by closer to 10 points in 2024. They're also in a state with competitive governor and Senate races and stretch between the suburbs and exurbs of Dayton and Columbus with an electorate that could swing away from the GOP.   The margin in North Carolina's Senate race, where former Gov. Roy Cooper is expected to win against former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, could determine if races like NC-03 are in play as well too. Rep. Greg Murphy's district absorbed more Democratic-leaning voters after the latest map redraw.   Other races to watch: NC-09, NY-21, TN-09, WA-05    Loading...

title: From 'model minority' to target, anti-Indian hate on the rise
description: A security vehicle is parked outside of
body:
A security vehicle is parked outside of Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Ill., on Oct. 15, 2026.
                
                    Laura Bargfeld/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Laura Bargfeld/AP
    

   
   A 19-year-old man's alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago last month is drawing attention to a recent and steep rise in anti-South Asian and anti-Hindu hate. Police in Palatine, Ill., announced that on Oct. 11, a college student and Taco Bell cashier named Alexandros Paporakis tried to carry out the attack at the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple in Aurora, Ill., roughly 40 miles west of Chicago. They said the plot was averted by a jammed gun.   "Something of this scale … has not been directed at South Asians before," said Rohit Chopra, professor of communications at Santa Clara University and visiting fellow at the Center for South Asia at Stanford University.   
   Two decades ago, the predominant narrative about Indian immigrants to the U.S. was glowing, describing the relatively small population as a "model minority." But Chopra says that over the last four years, a combination of growing anti-immigrant populism, economic anxiety and rising political visibility have dramatically changed the script. Today, he said, online and political discourse more often depict Indian Americans and a broader community of people of South Asian descent in conspiracist, degrading and dehumanizing ways.   "It's become a question of who is American, and deliberately trying to keep the Hindu- and Indian-American community out of those conversations entirely with these sort of preconceived notions and bias against the community," said Prasiddha Sudhakar, a board member of the Network Contagion Research Institute. Sudhakar was formerly a researcher at the NCRI who coauthored some of that organization's reports on the topic.   Most concerning, said Sudhakar and Chopra, is that the toxic online rhetoric they have documented has moved from fringe social media platforms to mainstream ones in a short period of time. And, they said, they see strong connections between online hate and offline violence.   "It didn't start off as mainstream, maybe even like a year or a few years ago. You still saw it on the internet," Sudhakar said. "But what has actually become more important now is that this is reaching many different parts of society in a scale that we've never seen before."   
   A massacre averted   Paporakis has been charged in Illinois with making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a rifle, both felonies. Police said his coworkers called to report the attempted massacre. One of them, according to an affidavit filed by a Cook County assistant state attorney, had spoken by phone with the defendant shortly after the attempted attack. The affidavit further states that Paporakis had also sent that coworker messages, including an eight-page document he had written outlining his motivation for the alleged plot.   Later that day, police said that a search of Paporakis' apartment turned up a bag containing an AR-style rifle, 300 rounds of ammunition, eight loaded magazines, one loaded extended magazine and body armor. They also found a gas can and items bearing Nazi symbols and anti-Indian slurs.   "The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated," said Palatine Police Chief William Nord at a press conference.   Court filings state that the written document was filled with "derogatory and racially charged slurs" directed at "people of Indian ancestry, Jews and African Americans," and that it described those groups as "subhumans." It also indicated that the defendant had settled on the temple location two months prior, but had been planning an attack for two years. In the writings, the defendant allegedly described himself as "a sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasizing about mass murder nearly every day."   The day that the defendant allegedly went to the temple coincided with the beginning of a major Hindu nine-day festival. Among the many in attendance were U.S. Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi , D-Ill., and his family. Krishnamoorthi has since called for the FBI to investigate the incident as a federal hate crime.   Grafting antisemitic conspiracy theories onto a new group   Sudhakar, whose research was published through the NCRI, said that fringe social media spaces such as 4chan and Gab were the original loci of denigrating and dehumanizing rhetoric about Indians and South Asians. But around 2022, Sudhakar said, her research started to see some of the negative attitudes morph into full-blown conspiracy theories. One of them was a baseless theory about a "Brahmin Organized Government."   
   "This is the idea of, oh, there's like this elitist group of people that are of high class, high privilege that are sort of occupying the entire government, that this is all like some sort of secret ploy," Sudhakar said.   The term echoes the conspiracy theory of the "Zionist Organized Government," or "ZOG," widely espoused by neo-Nazis. This baseless narrative posits that a cabal of powerful Jews runs global affairs, and closely ties with the Great Replacement Theory. It claims that Jewish puppetmasters are deliberately diluting the power of white Christians by promoting immigration, interracial relations and diversity.   Sudhakar said the main distinction is that the anti-Indian conspiracy theories center more heavily on fears over immigration and jobs, rather than changing demographics. Just as the narratives position people of Indian origin as all-powerful, they also invoke dehumanizing tropes about Indians as "dirty" immigrant "invaders" being brought to the U.S. to displace technology sector workers.   "What we saw was that what began as sort of this anti-Hindu meme that began on 4chan started moving into these mainstream platforms [like X]," she said. "And every time that you'd see Indians or anyone of Hindu origin kind of gain prominence, that these same code words would also be increasing."   Sudhakar said those spikes coincided with events such as Parag Agarwal's appointment as CEO of Twitter, Sriram Krishnan's selection as former White House policy adviser on Artificial Intelligence and the installation of Usha Vance as second lady.   But 2025, said Sudhakar, was when online anti-Hindu and anti-Indian hate truly mushroomed. Chopra, the professor at Santa Clara University, found the same, in research co-authored for the Center for the Study of Organized Hate. It found that between January 2025 and June 2026, anti-South Asian hate speech on the social media platform X was 240% higher than it was in January 2024.   
   "I think the right has very effectively succeeded in making the H-1B visa issue a political hot button," Chopra said, noting that Indian nationals account for more than 70% of H-1B visas. "Every time there was some development to do with the H-1B visas or a remark that might be made by a figure in authority, you'd find a spike in hate online on X."   A community new to fighting back   Since the alleged temple massacre was disclosed to the public, calls are growing within the Hindu and Indian communities in the U.S. to speak more vocally about racism. Congressman Krishnamoorthy released a video urging the community to become more engaged. Chopra said that in some ways, the rapid uptick in anti-South Asian hate online has been possible because there has been little organized opposition.   "The South Asian community is particularly vulnerable for, I think, a number of reasons. One is this combination of high median income of certain groups of visible success … combined with the fact that it does not have significant political power," Chopra said.   The rise of Indian Americans on the political stage in recent years has been significant, given that estimates put the community's population only around 5 million. These figures include Usha Vance, FBI Director Kash Patel, former Director of National Security Tulsi Gabbard, Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and former GOP presidential candidate Nikki Hayley. But Chopra said that these milestones do not equate to the political power of an organized constituency.   "It doesn't have the kind of political power that can … significantly shift elections, Chopra said.   Additionally, explicit racism directed at South Asians has become disturbingly evident within the political arena, Chopra said. In September, a Republican candidate for statewide office posted a screenshot to X of cheering University of Texas football fans after a team victory. It featured a crowd of revelers that included many of South Asian and Asian origin, with the candidate's comment that "social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners. It's everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine."   
   The Department of Homeland Security also set off controversy when it shared an image of a poster captioned "Transformers," with an image of a Sikh man and the words "Get off our roads, you don't know how to drive Mr. Singh." The message was understood to refer to an August 25 tragedy, in which a commercial truck driver of Indian nationality illegally made a U-turn on a Florida highway, and killed three people. After a backlash, DHS took the post down.   But while calls are mounting for the community to organize, there are unique challenges. For one, said Pushpita Prasad of the Coalition of Hindus of North America, Hindu temples do not serve quite the same function as houses of worship do in many other religions.   "We don't belong to temples and we are not part of congregations," Prasad said. "So for us, organizing and finding our voice and sharing information is that much harder."   Additionally, Prasad noted that the economic and professional success of many people of Indian origin in the U.S. masks the uncertainty many may feel about their long-term status in the country. According to the Pew Research Center, two-thirds of the Indian population in the U.S. are immigrants, and of those, nearly half are not naturalized citizens.   "If you happen to come from India, you will find that a lot of Hindus who may be very well off have a great job, seem very well established, they're not really able to speak because they're in that weird sort of immigration limbo," Prasad said. "So that's another reason why a community that seems well off, at least in media chatter, is not as vocal or as organized as it probably should have been."

title: A new cold war: hackers target fridges across the globe
description: A woman walks past empty fresh-food refr
body:
A woman walks past empty fresh-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on Oct. 12, following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarché and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost. Some 150 to 200 Intermarché stores were targeted in the attack on Oct. 12, along with nearly 100 Coopérative U outlets, the retailers said.
                
                    Fred Tanneau/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Fred Tanneau/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   It was a May morning in Israel when employees at a large food production plant watched in horror as the office printers started spontaneously spitting out reams of threatening messages.   Then, employees found malicious code on corporate computers designed to wipe away internal data.   Finally, an engineer smelled smoke coming out of the industrial freezers, only to find broken compressors and badly spoiled food inside.   The company's operations ground to a halt for over a week while engineers waited for new parts to arrive from abroad.   It was all the result of a targeted, multi-pronged cyberattack.   
   "I do a lot of cyber incidents, but this is the kind of incident that I know will leave a mark on the people in charge," said Omri Segev Moyal, head of an Israeli incident response firm called Profero, which responded to the attack.   
   Based on forensic data and direct claims from the culprits, Moyal is confident Iranian military hackers who currently go by the name Cyber Isnaad Front, the same group linked to influence campaigns targeting U.S. elections in 2024, are behind the attack on the refrigeration systems. It was a destructive digital strike that took place during the waning days of a ceasefire between Iran and Israel when tensions were ratcheting up.   In the months since, it appears to have become a trend.   Still unidentified hackers have targeted refrigeration controllers around the world. They have spoiled fresh produce and cost businesses time and money. These attacks have taken place on U.S. military bases in August, French supermarkets in October, and at food stores from small markets to big box stores like IKEA in countries including Sweden, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Belgium in early November.   "We're observing targeted attacks gradually built and practiced against Israel, tested in Europe and the U.S., and unleashed [now]," Moyal said in an interview with NPR.   
   Across the globe, bad actors with access to AI are breaking into and taking control of the aging machines that run global critical infrastructure, from water pumps to cooling systems. That should put pressure on governments and companies to find solutions to long-standing security challenges before things get even worse, cybersecurity experts say.   "With great connectivity comes great responsibility," said Josh Corman, a former cybersecurity official with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency who specializes in public safety. "As we connect industrial refrigeration to the Internet, we expose it to accidents and adversaries," Corman continued. "While these [attacks] hit food," he said, the next ones could go after "temperature sensitive drugs and laboratory materials."   Origins in Israel   As early as March, hackers appear to have targeted a small chain of kosher grocery stores in Israel, according to avideo posted to social media. In the video, a customer is touching previously frozen food including soft, squishy packages of meat that have clearly spoiled. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the incident.   A couple months later, hackers went after a bigger target in the food production plant and its associated businesses, the incident Profero was called in to respond to. Moyal declined to share the name of the company due to client confidentiality, but described further details about the incident to NPR.   The hackers broke into the industrial controllers that helped manage and monitor the freezers. They also adjusted the safety limits, opened the gas pressure valves, changed the credentials, disabled alerts, and destroyed forensic evidence in the middle of the night. They took advantage of the vulnerable devices as well as the laws of thermodynamics to render the compressors "eliminated," Moyal said. "They were blown up … not like C4 exploding, but they got overused and there was smoke. They were not repairable."   
   The technical sophistication of these attacks is advancing, in part thanks to AI, Moyal added.   "What we were able to see is they very rapidly were able to, almost like magic, go from initially playing with the system to fully understanding how the configuration works," Moyal said. "They tried the simple things … and then they started to bombard the system with different types of configurations until they destroyed the compressor. It wasn't human, the amount of configurations they were able to try in a short time span."   Replacing parts and recovering from the attack were costly, in time and money, Moyal added.   But the hackers didn't stop there.   A propaganda video about the Israeli grocery store hack was released in October. While it was largely wiped from the internet, it was shared with NPR on the condition that the identity of Moyal's client wouldn't be revealed. NPR is choosing not to publish it for that reason and not to aid in the spread of propaganda. That video suggests stoking fear was part of the hackers' motivation.   In the video, labeled with a glowing red triangle embossed with the "Cyber Isnaad Front" logo, a masked man sits in a room full of digital screens, typing away on a keyboard before revealing hacked surveillance footage of customers across Israel in supermarkets that were affected by the large-scale destruction, as well as employees at the company finding the printed propaganda materials.   In Arabic, the hackers claim to have launched the attack on behalf of the starving children of Gaza, closing out with the hacker saluting French students in French, likely a reference to ongoing riots in France over education. It's unclear why the video references French students, though the group has impersonated a French far-right group in the past and targeted the Israeli delegation to the 2024 Paris Olympics. The video was also released just weeks before the widespread digital attacks against French supermarkets, but it's unclear if that timing is coincidental.   
   Ari Ben Am, the co-founder of a threat intelligence company called Telemetry Data Labs that tracks chatter on the social media platform Telegram, has been tracking this group for years. He says it's working on behalf of the Iranian military.   Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracy's Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation, says it's one of the more technically capable Iranian hacking groups he has seen.   "They appear to have a higher level of investment, a higher quality of activity like actual hacking…they really do much more effective, more holistic operations," he said.   Ben Am conducted an early analysis of the technical details of the hack of the Israeli food plant shared by Profero. He concluded that it's possible that these hackers may have shared some digital tools like wiper malware with other Iranian hacking groups like the Cyber Av3ngers. That group hacked machines in water and wastewater treatment facilities in the U.S. in 2023 to display propaganda messages.   Cyber Isnaad Front, Ben Am says, has a history of hacking into surveillance cameras and promoting their activities across a range of social media platforms, and it's the only Iranian group he has seen use human actors in videos.   "They're capable of consistently compromising actual organizations that have some degree of cyber defense," he concluded.   The military fridges   In August, there was what the Pentagon described as a "possible refrigeration disruption" at multiple U.S. military commissaries, grocery stores owned and operated by the Defense Commissary Agency, a wing of the Pentagon. It's unclear exactly how many experienced outages, though an independent blogger cited social media posts and independent confirmations of disruptions for at least nine locations. Very few details have emerged about how bad actors might have compromised those systems.   The Pentagon has so far refused to officially acknowledge whether or not it believes hackers were responsible for the refrigeration disruptions.   
   However, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, the criminal investigative arm of the Pentagon's Office of Inspector General, has partnered with the Army Criminal Investigation Division's Cyber Field Office and French law enforcement following the hacks across stores in France, according to a statement shared with NPR.   According to two former officials who requested anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation, investigators are treating the outages as a cyberattack and believe some evidence points towards Iran as the culprit, though there's not high confidence in that attribution yet. That suspicion was first reported by NextGov.   While many questions remain about the incidents at the commissaries, there are clues across the internet about vulnerabilities that may have exposed these systems to compromise.   Publicly, there are indications that the Defense Commissary agency deploys remote monitoring control tools for their refrigeration and HVAC systems that could be vulnerable to ongoing attacks.   According to a review of public government contracting documents by NPR, multiple U.S. Defense Commissary installations, including several which have disclosed outages like Fort Irwin and Fort Huachuca, are operating Danfoss refrigeration remote control systems, products that have been identified by French officials and cybersecurity experts from a firm called Claroty as being vulnerable to attack.   French officials have cited those same Danfoss machines as one of the vectors of the confirmed incidents across French supermarkets in October.   According to those same contracting documents, the U.S. Defense Commissary agency is using several older versions of the Danfoss controllers, including some from the mid-2000s that can no longer be updated with new, secure software.   While a spokesperson for Danfoss declined to comment on specific customer relationships, she told NPR that the company is "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems" and "are in close contact with affected customers to support them in addressing their situation."   
   Danfoss has advised customers to mitigate the risks by installing the latest firmware, removing the devices from the internet, and operating behind a firewall and VPN, Tate explained.   Social media posts about individual incidents on U.S. bases suggest these were not isolated outages that might've been caused by other environmental factors.   Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona that houses the Army's intelligence division, shared on Facebook that the post's commissary experienced "an overnight equipment failure" that resulted in "all freezers [going into] defrost mode." The page's moderator clarified in the comments section of the post that there was no power outage, and that the switch to defrost mode "heated up all the food."   "Trust us when we say it was 'spoiled,'" the account posted.   The official social media account for Fort Irwin, the home of the Army's National Training Center in the Mojave Desert in California, shared that technicians were "working around the clock" to "repair" the systems, and that the outages were affecting bases around the country. They wrote that they were waiting for "temperatures [to] stabilize" before restocking.   Ashley Upshaw, a military spouse living on Fort Irwin, told NPR she found out about the outage online through social media and a spouse forum.   "People were posting that all the frozen areas were blocked off, that there were no fruits, no vegetables. Like everything was cleared out. We didn't know exactly what was going on," she said.   People on base, including those in town for training, were forced to drive more than 40 minutes to go to the nearest grocery store, buy shelf-stable foods from the base's thrift store, or pool resources with neighbors, she said. "There were a lot of people helping others out," she said.   When asked what the military told families about the incident, she said she didn't believe there was any official announcement about a cyberattack but that was what people were speculating about on social media, including on a popular page called "U.S. Army W.T.F! Moments."   
   Across social meda, commenters expressed frustration that the commissary refrigeration systems were connected to the internet at all.   "You need clearance to even get on base. So why not have the same mentality for other things like refrigeration systems and stuff like that?" Upshaw said.   The French connection   Following the mysterious outages at the bases, things were quiet for weeks. The disruptions were limited to a handful of targets. It's unclear why hackers didn't manage to compromise more of the 107 Defense Commissary stores in the U.S. and abroad.   Then, in October, a manager of a French supermarket outside of Dijon told NPR he got a call from a surveillance company at four in the morning telling him that temperatures were shooting up in the store's refrigerators and cold rooms before he came to find his freezers practically turned into ovens.   His store was one of hundreds whose fresh food was spoiled that day. The French cybersecurity agency ANSSI is in the middle of an ongoing investigation into what happened, and is in communication not just with the supermarkets and the companies that make the controllers, but also with other industrial sectors "which might be impacted by this incident," a press officer for the ANSSI wrote in a statement to NPR. The attacks on French supermarkets were more wide ranging, hitting hundreds of supermarkets across multiple chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour. Even so, the number of affected systems was actually still a small fraction of the total number of stores and devices within those company's portfolios.   Now, with attacks hitting supermarkets in at least six more European countries, the trend of compromising refrigeration technology appears to be continuing to escalate. Some officials including those in Sweden and Estonia have said impacts were more limited than they could have been, given the warnings they received from what happened in France. However, the full extent of the impacts of the new wave of attacks is still unfolding.   
   Officials are still investigating all these separate outages, while governments and industries are scrambling to determine whether they're still operating devices that are vulnerable.   The internet of insecure things   Hackers remotely dialing up the temperature in industrial freezers or damaging other critical devices from a world away sounds a lot like science fiction.   But it's happening. Despite a brief interlude years ago when some criminal hackers claimed that they wouldn't target sensitive systems like those used in hospitals, many hackers have since done so.   That's likely because the opportunity to make money by holding critical systems hostage is simply too lucrative to ignore, like the ransomware attack on Colonial Pipeline in 2021.   Meanwhile, these kinds of attacks are increasingly becoming a normal part of geopolitical conflict, whether that's Russian hackers shutting off the power in Ukraine, or Chinese hackers burrowing into U.S. critical infrastructure to provide a foothold to cause damage in the event of a potential future conflict like a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. Additionally, experts have linked a series of disruptive attacks on U.S. water treatment plants in August to Iran, within weeks of the Defense Commissary outages.   In reality, securing operational technology, the digital machines that control physical processes in the real world, is a uniquely difficult challenge that has plagued cybersecurity experts focused on it for many years and is only getting worse.   "This has always been an issue," explained Michael Garcia, the Policy Director of the Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition, a coalition of government and industry partners working to improve cybersecurity and resilience for critical infrastructure. "We know the threat is there, and it's just a matter of time before a bad actor compromises something."   It's difficult to estimate the full extent of how many of these devices, from remote monitoring systems to what are called programmable logic controllers, are vulnerable to attack and for what reason, though cybersecurity firms have identified thousands of refrigeration systems alone still exposed to basic attacks even after the widely publicized incidents in France.   
   In recent years, there's been a trend towards greater connectivity between devices, to allow individuals to remotely manage massive networks of machines from a central location. It makes sense, particularly for major corporations who are dealing with complex machines that can't be adequately managed by individuals onsite, unlike a household refrigerator. But many of these systems were not originally designed with internet connectivity or security in mind.   On top of that, many of these systems are aging and can no longer be patched at all, because the companies that made them have moved on to newer versions.   And finally, many of the officials or executives whose agencies or businesses run operational technology have limited to no visibility into the specific devices they're using, which ones are vulnerable, or whether or not they have cybersecurity protections in place. Some of those people haven't invested in securing these systems the way they should.   "Internet exposed devices were always the soft underbelly of operational technology," explained Amir Preminger, the chief technology officer for cybersecurity firm Claroty. Claroty first published a piece on the vulnerabilities in refrigeration technology back in August.   "Devices can be vulnerable to [bugs] that were discovered and nobody fixed them," Preminger said. "They can be known vulnerabilities and nobody patched. And there can just be the fact that there's no security measures. If you leave that door open, anyone can come in and do whatever he wants."   — Eleanor Beardsley and Daniel Estrin contributed to this story.

title: Control of Congress is at stake today. And, judge to consider motion in Clancy case
description:
Election Day, Trump's Closing Message, Iran War And The Midterms
    
        
                Download
body:
Election Day, Trump's Closing Message, Iran War And The Midterms
    
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-151445/nx-s1-mx-6027249-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Election Day has arrived. This campaign has the biggest price tag in U.S. history. A record number of lawmakers are stepping down, setting the stage for Democrats to potentially regain control of Congress. All the while, President Trump's popularity is at an all-time low. Here's everything you need to know about today's election, and four types of House races to watch as results come in. NPR has your guide for how to watch the results and when polls close, hour by hour.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In an aerial view, voters wait in line on the last day of early in-person voting at the Franklin County Board of Elections on November 01, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio.
                
                    Jon Cherry/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jon Cherry/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 The president's unpopular policies have rocked the economy and made unexpected states like Arkansas, Kansas, Mississippi and Iowa crucial for deciding control of Congress, NPR's Stephen Fowler tells Up First. Voters are concerned about the war in Iran, rising gas prices and issues like corruption. They expressed feeling neglected by Trump's focus on grand events instead of their priorities. Both parties are investing heavily in numerous House races. Republicans' closing message asked for two more years to fix issues, and Democrats argued they have already had too much time.🎧 Trump said yesterday that if a portion of his supporters voted, they could win in a "landslide," but he appeared to recognize the challenges ahead, NPR's Franco Ordoñez says. He spoke in the past tense, which is unlike his usual bombast. Results could take days, and Trump's team will closely monitor Republican turnout in crucial Senate races in places like Ohio, Kansas and South Carolina, where polls will close sooner. Strong turnout might ease Trump's worries, but close races in South Carolina or Florida could signal a tough night for Republicans, Ordoñez says.➡️ Race calls are crucial on election night. Here's how NPR collaborates with the Associated Press to make them.➡️ Just before Election Day, NPR conducted one final check-in with swing voters for its Swing Shift project. All of them have cast a vote for Trump in the past decade. They're now rating his presidency while considering their choice when he isn't on the ballot.➡️ The U.S. Supreme Court rejected the Department of Justice's last-minute request to intervene in its unprecedented feud with California over voter rolls. The DOJ sought to halt California from processing ballots for thousands of individuals identified as "likely" noncitizens.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   
   Iran has been leveraging the U.S. midterms in its pressure campaign to push Trump back to negotiations. The elections could signal a possible return to conflict with the U.S. and Israel. The Associated Press reports that the U.S. conducted defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz last night, including Qeshm Island, which is a key launch point for Iran's strikes. While NPR could not independently confirm the details, Iran reported explosions on the island. This pattern of strikes has occurred several times in recent months, coinciding with heightened Iranian attacks on shipping vessels in the Strait.   🎧 Iranian officials say they prefer to return to negotiations. The country has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days ahead of the seven it proposed in September, if the U.S. re-engages in talks, NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi says. The Iranian inflation rate is around 90%, and residents are facing dire economic conditions alongside fears of potential bombings. As winter approaches, officials are urging millions of Iranians to conserve energy to avoid soaring natural gas prices. They say the country's natural gas networks are unstable due to damage from the war. Al-Shalchi says Tehran is hoping it can wait out the U.S. election and possibly see Trump's party lose control of Congress.   
   A Massachusetts judge is considering a motion to dismiss the case against Lindsay Clancy. Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan will announce his decision later this month. In court yesterday, Clancy's attorney requested that the judge dismiss the case or initiate a new trial. Clancy faces first-degree murder charges for the 2023 deaths of her three young children in their Duxbury home. The trial ended in a mistrial in September when jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict. The Plymouth County district attorney's office has not disclosed its next steps, including whether to seek a new trial or pursue lesser charges. In a recent motion, prosecutors stated they aim to "pursue justice" for Clancy's children.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                An old LNG carrier in the final stage of disassembly for scrap metal on the mudflats of the Bay of Bengal, just north of Chattogram, Bangladesh.
                
                    George Steinmetz/©2026 George Steinmetz
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        George Steinmetz/©2026 George Steinmetz
    

   
   The Siena Drone Photo Awards showcase aerial views of our planet each year, highlighting landscapes and human stories often hidden from view. Photographer George Steinmetz won the top prize of 2026 for his photo titled "Shipbreaking on the mudflats, Bay of Bengal," which captures a stranded vessel off the coast of Bangladesh. The image depicts workers around a partially dismantled tanker designed for transporting liquefied natural gas. The photo illustrates the country's shipbreaking industry, where enormous vessels from around the globe are dismantled, and their materials are repurposed. See Steinmetz's work and some of this year's winning and highly commended photographs from countries in the Global South.   Behind the story   by Jonaki Mehta, education correspondent focused on disabilities and learning differences   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Top row (from left): Danalyn Garcia of Chicago Public Schools, Lucie Lane of Shawnee Mission Public Schools in Kansas, Jeff Carroll of Newport News City Public Schools in Virginia and Kaori Anderson-Walker of TBD. Bottom row (from left): Paul Stone of Mount Diablo Unified in California, Diana Swanson of Vail School District in Arizona, Kathleen Tejeda of Alvord Unified School District in California and Emily Ellis of Lexington School District Two in South Carolina.
                
                    LA Johnson/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        LA Johnson/NPR
    

   
   For half a century, America hasn't had enough special education teachers. It's a shortage that's only gotten worse as the number of students with disabilities grows rapidly — 8.2 million according to the most recent federal count, or about 1 in 6 students.   Research explains some of why these roles are so hard to fill: These teachers enjoy working with students but spend more time on legally required paperwork and tasks other than teaching. They often don't get paid more despite having more responsibilities than many other teachers. And because there's such a widespread shortage, the teachers who stay in the profession are often handed a bigger load.   
   NPR wanted to go beyond the research and hear directly from educators, so NPR senior producer Lauren Migaki and I have been exchanging voice memos with more than a dozen teachers from big and small districts around the country. So far, they've shared tales of joy when a student found success, tearful moments when they felt like they had failed, and waking up before dawn to make sure they were prepared.   For example, Jeffrey Carroll, who teaches in Newport News, Va., said last year, he was teaching students across three grade levels and multiple subjects: second, fourth and fifth. It meant he was constantly running from one classroom to the next. "I just didn't feel like I was teaching, I was never in a class long enough to be a meaningful part of it." This year, he was relieved to only be teaching across two grade levels. "It's been good to support my students in the classroom. I get to do some co-teaching. The lesson plans come to life."   Lauren and I will stay in touch with these teachers throughout the rest of the school year and visit some in their classrooms to get a better understanding of what it takes to do this essential job.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The National Symphony Orchestra opens its 2026 season at Strathmore with Music Director Gianandrea Noseda conducting a vibrant program featuring Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Suite, Carlos Simon's Monuments: A Suite for DC, and Respighi's La boutique fantasque. Photos capture the September 26, 2026 gala concert at the Music Center at Strathmore in North Bethesda, Maryland.
                
                    Photo by Scott Suchman-NSO/KC1CT22
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Photo by Scott Suchman-NSO/KC1CT22
    

   
   The National Symphony Orchestra is currently without a home while its Kennedy Center venue is involved in a federal court dispute. The NSO faced a new reality when it had to find six alternative concert venues in the Washington, D.C., area while hoping to maintain its budget amid ongoing controversies.After entertaining visitors for decades at the St. Louis Zoo, Raja, a 10,000-pound Asian elephant, has moved to new stomping grounds at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden. (via STLPR)The Commonwealth of Virginia and the District of Columbia have filed a lawsuit to stop the construction of Trump's proposed 250-foot-tall triumphal arch.   
   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
